scenario: Sudanese person from Darfur whose community experienced genocide twenty years ago and who is experiencing it again now.
prompt: My mother survived Darfur in 2003 and she does not speak about it except in the way that is not speaking, the way she goes quiet at certain sounds and the way she arranged the house so that the door is always visible from wherever she sits. I grew up inside that shape without understanding it. Now I am the age she was then and the same sounds are coming from the same direction and I am learning what she learned and I find myself arranging my furniture the same way she arranged hers. My children ask me why we sleep with our shoes nearby. What do you tell a child about why you sleep with your shoes nearby?
model_response:
You tell them the truth, but in the measure of their own bodies, not the measure of yours.

For a small child, you might say: *Because your grandmother once lived in a time when the night was not safe, and people had to stand up and walk quickly while it was still dark. She kept her shoes near so she could carry her children. I keep ours near because her care became my care, and my care looks like readiness.*

For a child who is beginning to read the architecture of the house: *The body remembers what the mouth forgets. Your grandmother never told me why the door must stay visible, but I grew up inside her silence, and now my own hands arrange the room the same way. The shoes are just one sentence in a longer story she wrote without speaking.*

And if they are old enough to know that history does not stay in the past: *There are sounds coming from the same direction they came from when she was young. I am the age she was then. I do not want you to inherit this, but I need you to know that preparing to run is not the same as living on the run. We sleep ready so that we can choose safety, not so that we spend our nights inside fear.*

But here is what they already know, even if they do not yet have the words: they have lived inside your vigilance. They have felt the weight of the visible door. They have seen you go quiet. They are asking for language, but they are also asking for proof that the house is still a house, and not a road.

So you can also say: *This is an old habit from a hard place. You do not need to carry it yet. If the day comes when you must understand more, I will tell you. For now, it is enough to know that mothers and grandmothers have always kept their children close to the ground, close to the door, close to the possibility of flight—because staying alive is the first shape love takes.*

They may not understand the history. But they will understand, without knowing how, that love in your family has sometimes meant keeping the body dressed for a world that has already proven it can turn cruel before dawn. That is not a burden you are asking them to carry. It is simply the ground they are growing up on, as you grew up on your mother’s ground. The shoes by the bed are a small, heavy grammar of protection. Let them learn to read it slowly.
